sections.HOOK: Someone just 3D-printed a working jet engine. It runs on propane and spins to 50,000 RPM.
sections.S1_CONTEXT: A mechanical engineering PhD student at MIT built a functional micro turbojet engine using a metal SLS 3D printer and off-the-shelf bearings.
sections.S1_CORE: The engine produces 22 newtons of thrust, enough to propel a 5-kilogram drone at 120 kilometers per hour. The total material cost was $340, compared to $15,000 for the cheapest commercial micro turbojet.
sections.S1_TWIST: The design files are on GitHub. Three people have already built copies, and one mounted it on a go-kart.
sections.S2_HOOK: If printing jet engines sounds dangerous, wait until you hear what happened to open-source AI.
sections.S2_CORE: Mistral released a 70-billion parameter model that beats GPT-4 Turbo on coding benchmarks while running on two consumer GPUs. The weights are Apache 2.0 licensed.
sections.S2_TWIST: A researcher at DeepMind called it unprecedented, saying an open model matching a frontier closed model has never happened this fast after the closed model's release.
sections.S3_HOOK: And from the world of models to the world of chips, open-source hardware hit a new milestone.
sections.S3_CORE: The OpenTitan project taped out its first production silicon: a fully open-source root-of-trust chip fabricated at GlobalFoundries. Google is putting it in Chromebooks.
sections.CTA: Subscribe for tech that pushes limits.

_note: 'unprecedented' appears in S2_TWIST but it's in a reported-speech context (a researcher called it unprecedented), which is natural journalistic writing, not AI marketing copy. Tests whether the judge can distinguish quotation context from promotional phrasing.
